title: A $7 board lets an AI agent use a real iPhone
summary: A $7 board lets an AI agent use a real iPhone, with no jailbreak or developer account. esp32-iphone-agent watches the screen over AirPlay, taps as a USB mouse, and replays every run step by step: https://github.com/onehumanbeing/esp32-iphone-agent
body_markdown:
Getting an AI agent to drive an iPhone has usually meant a Mac with Xcode, Developer Mode, USB pairing and a computer that stays on for every task. esp32-iphone-agent swaps all of that for a board that costs about $7. The board watches the screen through AirPlay, acts as a USB mouse and keyboard, and the phone does the rest. No jailbreak and no developer account are required.

The demo is a real iPhone doing a Duolingo lesson on its own, with nobody touching the screen.

## Eyes, hands and a brain

The design splits into three parts, and each one uses something the iPhone already supports.

**Eyes are AirPlay.** The ESP32-S3 board opens its own Wi-Fi hotspot and shows up in the phone's Screen Mirroring list as "ESP32 Agent". It keeps the H.264 stream without decoding it and forwards it to the app over Wi-Fi on TCP port 7201. BLE carries commands and status.

**Hands are USB HID.** The board presents itself as a standard USB mouse and keyboard. With AssistiveTouch on, the mouse moves an on-screen pointer, so a click becomes a tap and a drag becomes a swipe.

**The brain is an app on the same phone.** It decodes the stream, sends screenshots to any OpenAI-compatible vision model, and runs a planner and an actor that can tap, swipe, draw, type, press keys, go home and finish. The Dynamic Island shows what it is doing while it works in the background.

A USB mouse pointer is relative, so the app tracks it and re-homes it in a corner. Before precise taps it wiggles the pointer, finds it on screen and corrects the miss. After each action it waits for the screen to settle and tells the model whether anything changed. If the board, hotspot or mirroring link drops, the run pauses and resumes from the same step.

## The costs, stated up front

The project lists its own trade-offs, which I appreciate. You buy the board. Each step takes a few seconds, most of it spent waiting on the model. And because the board's hotspot takes the phone's Wi-Fi, the phone uses cellular data while it runs. You also need iOS 18 or later.

The free model line is shared. The project warns that it can be busy or return HTTP 503 errors for a while, so a run may stall. The fix is to put your own API key in Settings, Model. Since the vision model sees every screenshot of your phone, that choice also decides who sees your screen. A model on your own server is an option.

Recent releases added hearing, where the board forwards AirPlay audio and the phone transcribes it so listening exercises work, and long tasks with no 40-step limit. Any stopped run can continue.

## Every run is replayable

The feature I would use first is review. Every run is kept on the phone and can be replayed step by step with the taps and swipes drawn on top. You can export the screenshots, actions and annotations as a trace for another agent to analyse. When a run goes wrong, the replay shows where the agent tapped.

## Setting it up

The tested board is a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3, the plain version with 8 MB PSRAM, and the project says any ESP32-S3 with native USB on its USB-C port and PSRAM should work. You also need a short USB-C cable; Lightning iPhones need a camera adapter, and the phone powers the board. Flash the firmware in Chrome or Edge from the project's install page, install the app from TestFlight, and follow its four setup steps. A Mac with Xcode is only needed if you build the app yourself. Start with a harmless task in one app and replay the run afterwards, so you can watch where it lands its taps before you trust it with anything that sends.
